name: Snap-on smile
summary: A removable snap-over smile appliance from DenMat; documented in dental case reports as a temporary fix, with no trials behind it.
lead: Snap-On Smile is a removable cosmetic dental appliance made by the dental company DenMat. It is a thin tooth-borne overdenture that fits over a person's existing teeth, and is described in the dental literature as a temporary esthetic option rather than a permanent restoration . In appearance culture, the term is also used generically for removable "fake veneers" that snap over the natural teeth.

name: Fake tooth caps / press-on veneers
summary: DIY removable covers for the teeth; no studies on them exist.
lead: Press-on veneers and fake tooth caps are non-prescription cosmetic covers that are placed over the front of the teeth to change their apparent shape or shade, and are usually removable. They differ from dental veneers, which are thin layers of composite or porcelain bonded to the tooth by a dentist .

name: DIY braces with rubber bands / paperclips
summary: Improvised home tooth-moving with bands or wire; no research exists on it.
lead: DIY braces refers to attempts to move teeth at home using improvised materials such as rubber bands or bent wire, without a clinician's supervision. It is discussed as a low-cost alternative to orthodontic treatment.

name: DIY gap bands
summary: Home elastic bands aimed at closing tooth gaps; no studies exist.
lead: DIY gap bands are small elastic bands that people place around teeth at home in an attempt to close the gap between front teeth (a diastema) without seeing a dentist.

name: Chewing hard foods for jaw
summary: Chewing tough foods to bulk up the jaw muscles; untested for looks, with a possible jaw-joint association.
lead: Chewing hard foods for the jaw is a practice in which people chew tough or hard items, with the aim of building the masseter muscles and a more defined jawline. Proponents tie it to the belief that chewing grows the jaw muscles.

name: Jawline exerciser (Jawzrsize)
summary: A resistance chewing device marketed for jaw definition; no studies on the product exist.
lead: Jawline exercisers such as Jawzrsize are handheld devices that users bite or chew against with resistance, marketed to strengthen the jaw muscles and define the jawline.

name: Orthodontic extractions debate
summary: The long-running split over pulling teeth to straighten the rest, now amplified online by the anti-extraction orthotropic narrative.
lead: The orthodontic extractions debate concerns whether teeth, usually premolars, should be removed to resolve crowding and improve the facial profile, or whether space should instead be created by other means such as arch expansion. It is one of the oldest disputes in orthodontics. Edward Angle and his followers strongly opposed extraction and believed ideal occlusion would also yield good facial aesthetics, while Charles Tweed and Raymond Begg reintroduced extraction in the 1940s and 1950s to improve aesthetics and the stability of results . Teeth are reportedly extracted in about half of cases today, most commonly premolars .
claims: Extractions shrink the arches and flatten the face.
Crowding can be solved by expansion instead of extraction.

name: Invisalign attachments / chewies
summary: Small bonded bumps and rubbery bite cylinders that help clear aligners grip and seat; useful accessories with little dedicated research.
lead: Attachments are small tooth-colored composite shapes bonded to certain teeth during clear aligner treatment. They help the aligner rotate or pull down teeth, since the plastic is less rigid than metal . Chewies are soft cylinders that wearers bite on to help seat an aligner; they are an informal accessory and are not covered in the encyclopedic sources reviewed.

name: Retainer wear nightly
summary: Wearing a retainer at night after braces or aligners to hold teeth in place; orthodontic sources describe relapse risk as lifelong.
lead: Retainers hold teeth in corrected positions after orthodontic treatment. Orthodontic sources state there is a lifelong risk of relapse because of periodontal fibre recoil, soft-tissue pressure, the bite and continued growth . More than 50% of patients show some reversion within 10 years .

name: Wisdom tooth removal
summary: Surgical extraction of third molars, a routine procedure that looksmaxxers debate when it comes to crowding and jaw development.
lead: Wisdom teeth are the rearmost molars and typically erupt between about 17 and 21 . They are the most commonly impacted teeth, and impaction can lead to decay, gum disease and pericoronitis . Impacted teeth are usually extracted to treat or prevent such problems, and some clinicians have also removed them to prevent orthodontic crowding, which is disputed .
claims: Expansion can make room for wisdom teeth so removal is avoided.

name: Dental tourism (Turkey, Hungary, Mexico)
summary: Travelling abroad for cheaper cosmetic dental work, with documented savings and documented follow-up and liability concerns.
lead: Dental tourism is travel abroad for dental care. It is a subset of medical tourism, and Hungary, Turkey and Mexico are among the popular destinations . Researchers identify high local cost, delays in access, inexpensive air travel and the internet as drivers .

name: Floss
summary: String for cleaning between teeth: recommended by dental associations, with systematic reviews rating the evidence low certainty.
lead: Dental floss is a thread, usually nylon or silk, used to clean between the teeth. It comes waxed or unwaxed, monofilament or multifilament, with tape, picks, threaders and powered flossers as alternatives . The American Dental Association recommends daily flossing before or after brushing .

name: Interdental brushes
summary: Tiny brushes for the gaps between teeth; reviews link them to less plaque and gum inflammation than brushing alone.
lead: Interdental brushes are small, bristled brushes, usually on a short handle, designed to pass through the gaps between teeth and around orthodontic hardware to remove plaque from surfaces a regular toothbrush reaches poorly. They are sold over the counter in graded sizes, typically alongside floss, picks and similar devices.

name: Chlorhexidine mouthwash
summary: The reference antiplaque rinse; well studied for plaque, but staining and taste change come with it.
lead: Chlorhexidine mouthwash is an antiseptic oral rinse, generally in the 0.05 to 0.2 percent range, used as an adjunct to toothbrushing to reduce dental plaque and gingivitis. Chlorhexidine itself came into medical use in the 1950s and is on the World Health Organization Essential Medicines List.

name: Cetylpyridinium chloride mouthwash
summary: The standard drugstore antibacterial rinse; modest added plaque benefit, weaker than chlorhexidine, with some staining.
lead: Cetylpyridinium chloride (CPC) mouthwash is an over-the-counter antiseptic rinse built around a quaternary ammonium compound that kills bacteria and disrupts the membranes of enveloped viruses. Typical products contain about 0.05 percent CPC and are sold for plaque, gingivitis and bad breath.

name: Zinc mouthwash (TheraBreath)
summary: A zinc and chlorine dioxide breath rinse; zinc has trial data for mouth sores, but none found for this product on breath.
lead: Zinc-containing mouthwashes, including the TheraBreath line marketed for bad breath, combine zinc ions with other agents such as chlorine dioxide to bind or neutralise the volatile sulphur compounds that cause oral malodour. Wikipedia notes zinc is used with other antiseptics in rinses, and that zinc formulations with chlorhexidine stain less.

name: Alcohol-free mouthwash
summary: Mouthwash without ethanol, usually for dry-mouth comfort; effectiveness depends on the active ingredient.
lead: Alcohol-free mouthwash is a category of oral rinse formulated without ethanol, often with cetylpyridinium chloride, essential oils, herbal extracts or other active ingredients. Wikipedia notes many newer products omit alcohol partly over concern about a possible link to oral cancer, which it describes as inconclusive, and to suit people who avoid alcohol.

name: Essential oil mouthwash (Listerine)
summary: The classic Listerine-style rinse; reduces plaque and gingivitis modestly, with CHX still stronger on plaque.
lead: Essential oil mouthwash is a rinse whose active ingredients are thymol, menthol, eucalyptol and methyl salicylate, best known as Listerine. Listerine was developed in 1879 by St. Louis chemist Joseph Lawrence and named after surgeon Joseph Lister.

name: Chlorine dioxide rinse
summary: An oxidizing alcohol-free mouthwash aimed at breath odor; a small trial base, and not to be confused with the toxic chlorine-dioxide 'cure' products.
lead: A chlorine dioxide rinse is an alcohol-free mouthwash that contains stabilized chlorine dioxide, an oxidizing agent, as its active ingredient. It is marketed mainly for oral malodor (bad breath), and its proponents say it works by chemically neutralizing the volatile sulfur compounds (VSCs) responsible for much of the odor.

name: Oral probiotics (BLIS K12)
summary: Probiotic lozenges built around S. salivarius K12, pitched for fresher breath; thin human evidence for that use.
lead: Oral probiotics are live-bacteria products, typically lozenges, intended to colonize the mouth and throat. BLIS K12 is the best-known example in breath-focused discussion; it contains Streptococcus salivarius K12, a strain that produces bacteriocin-like inhibitory substances (BLIS).

name: Streptococcus salivarius K12
summary: A bacteriocin-producing oral probiotic sold in lozenges for bad breath; the breath evidence is one small preliminary study.
lead: Streptococcus salivarius K12 is a strain of a common oral bacterium sold as an oral probiotic, usually in lozenge form and often under the BLIS K12 name. It is promoted for bad breath (halitosis) and for supporting throat and oral health.

name: Zinc lozenges
summary: Cold-remedy lozenges that some breath-focused users take to neutralize sulfur compounds; the cold data is mixed and the breath use is untested.
lead: Zinc lozenges are dissolvable tablets containing a zinc salt, most often zinc gluconate or zinc acetate. They are best known as a common cold remedy, and some people in oral-care circles also use them in the belief that zinc neutralizes the sulfur compounds behind bad breath.

name: Xylitol gum
summary: Xylitol-sweetened gum that trials link to lower plaque bacteria; benefits beyond plaque are less settled.
lead: Xylitol gum is chewing gum sweetened with xylitol, a sugar alcohol, rather than sugar. It is promoted for reducing cavity-causing bacteria and plaque and for stimulating saliva.

name: Xylitol mints
summary: Sugar-free mints sweetened with xylitol; only lab-model evidence so far.
lead: Xylitol mints are breath mints sweetened with xylitol instead of sugar, used by people who want fresh breath without feeding oral bacteria and who want to stimulate saliva.

name: Sugar-free gum
summary: Sugar alcohol gum that boosts saliva and briefly freshens breath; dental trials are about cavities, not looks.
lead: Sugar-free chewing gum is gum sweetened with sugar alcohols such as xylitol, sorbitol, maltitol or isomalt, often with small amounts of intense sweeteners such as aspartame or sucralose. In oral-care and appearance discussions it is used mainly to freshen breath temporarily and to stimulate saliva, which dental researchers describe as protective for teeth.

name: Breath mints
summary: Minty candy that masks breath for a short while without addressing the cause.
lead: Breath mints are small mint-flavoured candies eaten to improve breath odour before or after social occasions. Wikipedia describes them as hard, soft or Scotch-style confections flavoured with mint or wintergreen oils. Dental sources and Wikipedia's halitosis article characterise mints and similar products as short-term masking rather than treatment of the cause of odour.

name: Breath strips
summary: Dissolving flavour films for a quick breath refresh; no trials on their effect.
lead: Breath strips are thin, flavoured films that dissolve on the tongue within moments and are sold to freshen breath. They use fast-dissolving film technology, which was developed as an oral delivery format for drugs and is described in pharmaceutical reviews as a film that dissolves in under a minute.

name: Parsley and mint chewing
summary: Folk habit of chewing fresh herbs for fresh breath; untested in trials.
lead: Chewing fresh parsley or mint leaves is a folk method for freshening breath, often after garlic- or onion-heavy meals. Parsley is widely used as a garnish and is described on Wikipedia as being credited in cooking with neutralising garlic odours.
claims: Chewing parsley or mint removes garlic breath

name: Chlorophyll tablets
summary: Chlorophyllin pills sold as internal deodorants; the one controlled odour trial found no difference from placebo.
lead: Chlorophyll tablets contain chlorophyll or, more often, chlorophyllin, a water-soluble semi-synthetic salt of chlorophyll used as a food colouring (E140 and E141). They are marketed as internal deodorants for breath, body, urine and faecal odour.
claims: Chlorophyll tablets reduce body and breath odour

name: Salt water rinse
summary: Warm salt-and-water home rinse used to soothe gums; compared with chlorhexidine in one school trial.
lead: A salt water rinse is a rinse of warm water with dissolved salt, used as a low-cost mouthwash for gum soreness and mouth hygiene. Wikipedia describes saline as a mechanical cleanser with antiseptic action because it is hypertonic to bacteria.
